source.title: Sparse is Enough in Scaling Transformers
source.authors: Sebastian Jaszczur; A. Chowdhery; Afroz Mohiuddin; Lukasz Kaiser; Wojciech P. Gajewski; H. Michalewski; Jonni Kanerva

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted results are described in the text but their underlying figure values are not available as text.
record.tranche_reason: It compares pretraining log-perplexity across sparse and dense Transformer architectures at matched parameter counts, bearing on whether architecture changes loss substantially. It does not test the scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation themselves.
record.gate_note: The reported C4 log-perplexity comparisons across sparse and dense architectures bear on V4. The paper also reports GLUE accuracy for these model variants, but does not relate those scores to model scale or pretraining loss; those results are recorded under fits_no_version. Decoding-speed results, toy-task generalization, and summarization results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares C4 pretraining log-perplexity of dense and sparse Transformers at matched parameter count (~800M). This bears on V4's idea that, at fixed parameters, architecture details change loss only slightly. The setting is new: sparse layers that cut per-token compute, not dense depth/width shape sweeps. The study was not designed as a scaling-law test, and nothing is swept over scale.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that fully sparse Scaling Transformers reach the same C4 perplexity as dense Transformers with the same parameter count while decoding much faster, with speedup benefits growing at 17B. They say Terraformer catches up to baseline perplexity with more steps, possibly held back by hyperparameters tuned for dense baselines.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of the scaling-law method: it compares dense and sparse Transformer architectures at matched parameter counts and reports perplexity, rather than fitting loss laws across parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss varies with feedforward sparsity (N=64 versus N=128) and Terraformer training checkpoint; the Terraformer checkpoints also use batch size 16 rather than the baseline batch size 4.

fits_no_version.finding: GLUE validation accuracy of dense, Scaling Transformer and Terraformer models at ~800M, with task-dependent differences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse variants at matched parameters reach GLUE accuracy comparable to dense; this is not a test of downstream predictability from scale or loss.

record.problems: The main C4 perplexity comparisons are reported in figures without numeric values in the text. The study tests selected architectures at approximately 800M parameters rather than a scale sweep. The authors also note that Terraformer used hyperparameters optimized for the baselines.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted. Decoding-time measurements, toy-task generalization, and summarization scores were excluded because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No sweep of depth, width, heads or aspect ratio in dense models. Only a single scale (~800M) is compared for loss, and the 17B models report decoding speed only.
Text-only; no other modalities or regimes.
GLUE is reported at one scale, not related to scale or loss.

missing.what: Mixture-of-Experts-style sparse FF log-perplexity of 1.64, worse than both Sparse FF and the dense baseline
Sparse loss layer with S=2,4,8 degrades perplexity slightly (figure only)

record.verdict_notes: The bearing on V4 is indirect. Sparse layers change per-token compute, not just shape, so equal loss at equal parameters is consistent with V4's parameter-count-centric view, but the evidence is at one scale. Most loss comparisons are figure-only. The paper cites Kaplan et al. but does not frame its results as a scaling-law test.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or sweep over parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No predictions from small runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token trend is tested.
The comparisons cover selected sparse/dense architectures and settings, not a broad systematic sweep of depth, width, and other architectural choices.
The study concerns text models and does not test whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
Downstream scores are reported, but the study does not test their predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves.

rows.subject: Baseline Transformer (dense)
rows.operation_detail: Dense architecture trained for the C4 log-perplexity comparison.
rows.note: The figure is described as showing the dense baseline and sparse variants with similar log-perplexity; no numeric value is given in the text.
rows.check: Comparator row. The dense baseline's log-perplexity is given numerically as 1.57 in Table 8, so the value can be filled in from there.

rows.subject: Scaling Transformer (Sparse FF, N=64)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with sparse feedforward layers, activating 1 in 64 entries per block at inference.
rows.note: The text says log-perplexity at N=64 is comparable to the baseline.

rows.subject: Scaling Transformer (Sparse FF, N=128)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with sparse feedforward layers, activating 1 in 128 entries per block at inference.
rows.note: The text says perplexity degrades slightly at N=128 relative to the baseline.
rows.check: The text says N=128 'degrades slightly'. A slight loss change at matched parameters is what V4 predicts, so this is observed, not partial.

rows.subject: Scaling Transformer (Sparse QKV)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with sparse QKV layers; the paper varies sparsity level S and kernel size F.

conditions.value: Sparse QKV; S and F varied

rows.note: The text describes the plotted Sparse QKV variants as very similar to the dense baseline within variance; separate numerical values for the S and F settings are not stated.

rows.subject: Scaling Transformer (multi-layer Sparse QKV)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with the multi-layer Sparse QKV variant shown in Figure 5.
rows.note: The text says the multi-layer variant improves perplexity; the plotted value is not stated numerically.

rows.subject: Scaling Transformer (Sparse FF+QKV)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with both sparse feedforward and sparse QKV layers.
rows.note: The text says the sparse models match the dense counterpart's performance; the plotted log-perplexity is not transcribed numerically.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 1 caption; Section 3.2, combined feedforward and QKV sparsity.

rows.subject: Baseline Transformer (dense)
rows.operation_detail: Dense baseline checkpoint in the Terraformer comparison.
rows.note: The table states that all compared models have the same parameter count and dimensions.

rows.subject: sparse Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained with sparse FF+QKV and the same sparse loss setting used for the Terraformer comparison.
rows.note: The sparse model is slightly higher in log perplexity than the dense reference.
rows.check: 1.61 vs 1.57 is a 0.04 gap at matched parameters and steps, which fits V4's 'only slightly'. This model also includes sparse loss (S=4).

source_check.locator_found: Appendix Section 6.5, Table 8, sparse Transformer row.

rows.subject: Terraformer
rows.operation_detail: Terraformer checkpoint trained with larger batches than the baseline.
rows.note: The authors say the larger-batch Terraformer does not match baseline perplexity at the early training point.
rows.check: At 125k steps × batch 16, Terraformer has seen the same number of sequences as the baseline at 500k × 4. The gap of 1.66 vs 1.57 is the matched-data comparison. Terraformer also changes attention (LSH), reversibility, recurrence and loss sparsity, and uses hyperparameters tuned for the baseline.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix Section 6.5, Table 8, Terraformer 125k row and caption.

rows.subject: Terraformer
rows.operation_detail: Terraformer checkpoint trained with larger batches than the baseline.
rows.note: This checkpoint remains above the dense reference in log perplexity.
rows.check: This checkpoint has seen 1.2x the baseline's data, so the condition is not matched in tokens.

rows.subject: Terraformer
rows.operation_detail: Terraformer checkpoint trained with larger batches than the baseline.
rows.note: This checkpoint is closer to the dense reference; the authors say Terraformer catches up at around one third of the baseline's training steps.
rows.check: This checkpoint has seen 1.4x the baseline's data. Its near-match (1.59 vs 1.57) is not at equal tokens.

source_check.correct: State: observed for the reported checkpoint's near-match under V4. Terraformer reaches 1.59 versus dense 1.57; the caption describes catching up around one third of the baseline's steps. This checkpoint uses 1.4 times the baseline's data and does not establish a matched-data near-match.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix Section 6.5, Table 8, Terraformer 175k row and caption.
source_check.problem: The 0.02 gap is a near-match, consistent with V4's slight loss differences; extra training data is a comparison caveat rather than evidence that this checkpoint's effect remains clearly incomplete.

relationships.condition: Sparse FF (N=64, N=128), Sparse QKV variants, Sparse FF+QKV, and sparse Transformer with sparse loss, all at ~800M params on C4
relationships.reason: Log-perplexity is described as comparable or slightly worse than dense (R2–R6). Table 8 gives 1.61 vs 1.57 (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Sparse variants had comparable or slightly worse log-perplexity than dense models, including a comparison of 1.61 versus 1.57.

source_check.condition: Sparse FF (N=64, N=128), Sparse QKV variants, Sparse FF+QKV, and sparse Transformer with sparse loss, all at ~800M params on C4
source_check.reason: R2–R6 are described as comparable, within variance, slightly degraded, or improved; R8 gives 1.61 versus 1.57. These results fit V4 in the tested architectures.

relationships.condition: Terraformer (LSH attention, reversible, recurrent, sparse loss) at matched training data; also MoE-style sparse FF (from text, no row)
relationships.reason: At equal data seen, Terraformer is at 1.66 vs 1.57 and needs more data to near-match (R9–R11). The text reports MoE-style FF at 1.64, 'worse than' dense. The authors attribute the Terraformer gap partly to untuned hyperparameters.
relationships.display_finding: Terraformer achieved loss 1.66 versus 1.57 and needed more data to approach the baseline, with its gap partly attributed to untuned hyperparameters, while MoE-style feed-forward layers achieved 1.64.
